description: A full team from Cairo, Egypt, combining programming, art, and science research skills. We’re focused on building something creative for NASA Space Apps 2026. No open spots at the moment, good luck to everyone!
summary:
Qamar 14 is a free 3D browser game that trains kids aged 7–12 as junior astronauts on a full round trip to Mars. It works on computers and phones, in Arabic and English.

The mission has seven stages: launch, Moon slingshot, crew health, building a Mars base, a solar storm, ascent and docking, and the return home. In each stage the child controls a different crew member. They make the decisions themselves through quick, simple challenges: choosing a safe weather window, steering a gravity assist, diagnosing fluid shift, growing lettuce under LED light, sheltering from radiation, and setting Orion’s parachutes in order.

Everything is built on real NASA science and data. The Mars terrain comes from HiRISE imagery of Victoria Crater, the solar storm is the real May 2024 X5.8 flare from DONKI, and the Moon, Sun and Earth come from LRO, SDO and Blue Marble. The game also teaches lessons from missions such as Phoenix, MOXIE, Veggie and Artemis. Mission Control on Earth sends messages that arrive late, about 1.3 seconds from the Moon and minutes from Mars, so children feel why astronauts must think for themselves.

The game turns real space science into play. It builds problem-solving, teamwork and curiosity, and lets kids see themselves as the future explorers of the Moon and Mars.
details:
What it does and how it works

Qamar 14 is a 3D browser game that turns a child aged 7–12 into the Captain of a crewed round trip to Mars. A short cinematic opening, narrated in English with Arabic and English subtitles, previews the journey. The player then completes seven stages seen from above, like a strategy game:

Launch from Kennedy Pad 39B

Moon gravity-assist slingshot

Crew health during the 7-month cruise

Building a Mars base

A real solar storm

Ascent and docking

Return and splashdown

In each stage the child controls a different crew member:

PICO, the robot assistant

Kiro, the engineer

Jana, the medical officer

Hekal, the resources scientist

the Captain

Each stage is a chain of short challenges. The child:

chooses a launch window under NASA’s lightning rule

steers a 2D gravity assist around the Moon

diagnoses fluid shift (SANS)

packs astronaut food

puts out a lab fire with sound waves (clearly labeled a research idea)

drills for ice and routes water into a radiation shield

splits water for oxygen

grows lettuce under red and blue LEDs

shares limited solar power between systems

shelters from the storm and repairs a comms dish using data

times the ascent and docks at 0.1 m/s

picks a safe entry angle

sequences Orion’s 11 parachutes

Mission Control on Earth (Adam and Nour) sends messages that visibly arrive late: about 1.3 seconds from the Moon and about 12.5 minutes from Mars, shown as a time-lapse. This teaches why crews must make their own decisions. Every challenge ends with a real NASA fact card and its source.

Real NASA data used

Mars terrain built from a HiRISE heightmap of Victoria Crater

The real May 2024 X5.8 flare and CME from DONKI

The Moon from LRO (LROC and LOLA)

The Sun from SDO/AIA

Earth from Blue Marble and Black Marble

Stars from NASA SVS

Mission facts from Phoenix, MOXIE, Veggie, FLEX, Artemis and Orion

A small backend fetches live NASA data and keeps the API key on the server, never in the browser. The game reads saved snapshots of that data, so it never hits NASA’s rate limits while children play.

Benefits and impact

Children learn real space science by doing it, not by reading it.

It builds decision-making, teamwork, problem-solving and data literacy.

Wrong answers explain why and let the child try again, so failure is safe.

It is free and runs on a phone or PC with no install.

It is fully bilingual: English, Arabic, or Arabic with English subtitles.

Our goal is to inspire Arabic- and English-speaking kids to see themselves as future Moon and Mars explorers.

Tools and technologies

Code: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS, built with Vite.

3D: three.js with custom shaders (animated Sun, CME, plasma, planets), plus GSAP for animation.

Backend: Node.js, TypeScript, Express and Zod, with automated tests in Vitest.

3D models: Blender, and Meshy AI for props.

Audio: Web Audio API sound effects, and Web Speech narration.

Music: an original celebration track composed in code with Python and NumPy, so there are no copyright issues.

Testing: Playwright automated playthroughs on desktop and mobile layouts.

Development: AI coding assistance (Claude).

Hosting: GitHub and Vercel.

Creativity

One story with seven playable crew roles, each with its own personality and humor.

Cinematic transitions between stages built from real NASA imagery.

The light-speed communication delay becomes a playable, visible moment, including a dance celebration at Mission Control when a signal arrives.

Kid-friendly humor makes real science memorable: the jerrycan that’s too heavy, the sofa in zero gravity, the disco lights for lettuce.

Factors we considered

Age fit: short, simple challenges for ages 7–12.

Scientific accuracy: on-screen notes say when sizes and distances are not to scale, when numbers are simplified learning models, and when an idea is still research.

Accessibility: mobile touch joystick, two languages, subtitles.

Performance on low-end phones.

Security: the NASA API key stays on the server.

Copyright and licensing: NASA public imagery, our own models, and original music.

Responsible data use: snapshots instead of live API calls during play.
